title: Peripheral IV Catheter Insertion
summary: Inserting a short peripheral IV catheter into a peripheral vein for medication/fluid administration.
steps: Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Identify appropriate vein — antecubital, forearm, or dorsal hand. Avoid areas of bruising, infection, or AV fistula side.
Apply tourniquet 4–6 inches above the insertion site.
Clean the site with chlorhexidine or alcohol swab using a circular or back-and-forth motion. Allow to fully dry.
Remove catheter needle cap. Bevel up, insert at 10–30° angle in the direction of blood flow.
Watch for flashback (blood in the catheter chamber). Once visible, lower the angle and advance 1–2mm further.
Slide the catheter off the needle while stabilizing the needle — do not reinsert needle once removed.
Release the tourniquet. Apply pressure proximal to the site with one finger while removing the needle.
Dispose of needle immediately in sharps container.
Attach extension set or cap. Flush with 10mL NS using a push-pause technique to confirm patency.
Apply transparent dressing (Tegaderm) and secure with tape. Label with date, time, gauge, and your initials.
Document site appearance, gauge, attempts, and patient tolerance.
nursing_considerations: Avoid the dominant arm, areas of edema, or the arm with a mastectomy.
If two attempts fail, have another nurse attempt or consider escalating.
Assess insertion site every shift for signs of infiltration, phlebitis, or infection.
Replace peripheral IVs per facility policy (typically every 72–96 hours).
Use smallest gauge appropriate for treatment — 18g for blood, 20–22g for general meds.

title: Peripheral IV Catheter Removal
summary: Safely removing a peripheral IV catheter when no longer needed or when complications arise.
steps: Verify order to discontinue IV or confirm IV is no longer needed.
Explain procedure to patient. Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Turn off any infusing fluids or clamp IV tubing.
Gently loosen and remove the dressing/tape securing the catheter. Avoid pulling on the catheter.
Place sterile gauze over the insertion site. Do NOT apply pressure yet.
Using a smooth, steady motion, withdraw the catheter parallel to the skin.
Immediately apply firm pressure with gauze for 2–3 minutes (longer for anticoagulated patients).
Inspect the removed catheter — confirm it is intact. Note the tip and length.
Inspect the site for hematoma, swelling, or redness.
Apply bandage or tape gauze in place. Instruct patient to keep bandage on for at least 30 minutes.
Dispose of catheter in appropriate sharps/biohazard container.
Document removal, site condition, catheter integrity, and patient tolerance.
nursing_considerations: Never reinsert a catheter once removed — risk of introducing contamination.
If catheter tip appears broken or missing, notify provider immediately and apply pressure — do not massage.
Apply pressure for at least 5 minutes for patients on anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin, aspirin).
If the site shows signs of phlebitis (redness, warmth, pain, streak), document and notify provider.
Warm compresses to the site post-removal can help resolve discomfort or localized phlebitis.

title: Central Line / PICC Dressing Change
summary: Performing a sterile dressing change on a central venous catheter or PICC line.
equipment: CVAD dressing change kit (includes sterile gloves, CHG disc/swab, transparent dressing, Steri-strips, mask)
steps: Review order and last dressing change date. Check for signs of infection or dislodgement.
Perform hand hygiene. Don clean gloves and mask. Apply mask to patient.
Carefully remove old dressing by stabilizing catheter hub — pull dressing parallel to skin toward insertion site.
Inspect site: redness, swelling, discharge, catheter migration (check external length vs. documented).
Remove clean gloves. Perform hand hygiene. Don sterile gloves.
Clean insertion site with CHG swab using a back-and-forth scrub motion for 30 seconds. Allow to dry 30 seconds.
Apply CHG disc (if used) around catheter at insertion site.
Apply transparent semipermeable dressing over site, starting at insertion point and pressing outward.
Secure catheter hub and tubing to prevent tension on the line.
Label dressing with date, time, and initials.
Document dressing change, site assessment, and external catheter length.
nursing_considerations: Change dressing every 7 days (transparent) or every 2 days (gauze) or when soiled/loosened.
Use CHG-based dressings when available — they significantly reduce CLABSI rates.
Never reinsert a migrated catheter — notify provider.
Assess for CLABSI signs: fever, rigors, erythema >2cm, purulent drainage.
Maintain strict sterile technique — central line infections are life-threatening.

title: Blood Transfusion Administration
summary: Safely administering packed red blood cells or other blood products to the patient.
steps: Verify provider order. Obtain signed informed consent if required by facility policy.
Retrieve blood product from blood bank no more than 30 minutes before administration.
Perform two-nurse verification at bedside: check patient name, DOB, MRN, blood type, Rh factor, unit number, expiration date, and product type against armband and blood bank tag.
Assess baseline vital signs: temperature, blood pressure, pulse, respirations, SpO2.
Ensure patent IV access — 18g or larger. Use a dedicated blood line (Y-tubing) primed with NS.
Hang NS on one arm of the Y-tubing. Hang blood product on the other arm. Prime the filter with NS.
Switch flow to blood product. Begin infusion SLOWLY for first 15 minutes (no faster than 2 mL/min).
Remain at bedside for first 15 minutes — most transfusion reactions occur early.
Recheck vital signs at 15 minutes. If stable, adjust rate to complete transfusion within 4 hours.
Monitor patient every 30 minutes during transfusion: vital signs, symptoms.
If any reaction signs appear (fever, chills, hives, back pain, hypotension, dyspnea) — STOP transfusion immediately, keep IV open with NS, notify provider, save blood bag.
Once transfusion complete, flush with NS. Document entire process and post-transfusion assessment.
nursing_considerations: ONLY use 0.9% NS with blood — Lactated Ringer's, D5W, or medications in same line can cause hemolysis.
Complete each unit within 4 hours of leaving blood bank — bacterial growth risk increases after this.
Premedicate with diphenhydramine or acetaminophen only if ordered — not routine prophylaxis.
Acute hemolytic reaction is the most dangerous reaction — caused by ABO incompatibility. Symptoms: fever, chills, back/flank pain, dark urine. Stop immediately.
Febrile non-hemolytic is the most common reaction — mild fever/chills. Slow/stop infusion, notify provider.

title: IV Piggyback (IVPB) Medication Administration
summary: Administering an IV medication via secondary/piggyback infusion through an existing IV line.
equipment: IV pole with extension hook (to lower primary bag)
steps: Verify the 5 rights of medication administration. Check medication compatibility with primary IV fluid.
Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Spike the IVPB bag with secondary tubing. Prime the secondary tubing with the medication.
Hang the IVPB bag on the primary IV pole. Lower the primary IV bag using the extension hook (or a secondary hook) so IVPB hangs higher.
Clean the upper secondary port on the primary IV tubing with an alcohol swab. Allow to dry.
Connect the secondary tubing to the upper port on the primary IV line.
Set the infusion pump for the correct IVPB rate and volume. Most IVPB medications infuse over 30–60 minutes.
Ensure the primary line is still patent and the IV site shows no infiltration or phlebitis.
Start the infusion. Verify the IVPB is infusing and primary fluid is on hold (automatic with gravity systems when IVPB is higher).
Monitor patient for adverse medication reactions during infusion.
Document medication, dose, time, route, and patient response.
nursing_considerations: Always verify drug-drug and drug-fluid compatibility before piggyback — many medications are incompatible.
Flush line with compatible fluid before and after IVPB if compatibility is uncertain.
Do not piggyback through a TPN (total parenteral nutrition) line — dedicated TPN lines should remain exclusive.
For antibiotics, infuse over the ordered time to ensure therapeutic drug levels and prevent toxicity.
Discard partial bags — never store and rehang a partially-infused IVPB bag.
